_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 172 - Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4: Legend of Aiai (pp. 554-558), Legend of Pupualenalena (pp. 558-560), Legend of Kaulanapokii (pp. 560-561), Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (pp. 596+). Topics 3 heroic, 8 trickster, 2 deity. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Aiai Regains the Pearl Hook Kahuoi
title.zh: 埃埃重奪珍珠神鉤卡胡奧伊

region.zh: 瓦胡島檀香山努瓦努尼奧洛帕

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Kuula and Hina, great fisher folk of Nuolopa, own the pearl hook Kahuoi, guarded by the bird Kamanuwai at Kaumakapili: every aku outside Mamala jumps into Kuula's canoe of its own accord. King Kipapalaulu steals the hook; the bird starves with closed eyes - hence the name Kaumakapili, roosting-with-closed-eyes. Their infant Aiai is cast into the stream, floats to the rock Nahakaipuami, and is reared by the king's daughter Kauaelemimo, whom he marries. Through her he tricks her father into producing the stolen hook from the fishermen's calabash, borrows a ten-fathom canoe, and fills it with aku that leap in of their own accord.
summary.zh: 庫拉與希娜居努瓦努尼奧洛帕，家藏珍珠神鉤卡胡奧伊，由神鳥卡馬努瓦伊守於考馬卡皮利：馬瑪拉外的鰆魚見鉤即自躍入舟。國王基帕帕勞盧竊鉤；神鳥閉目絕食——『考馬卡皮利』（閉目棲息）由此得名。嬰兒埃埃被擲入溪流，漂至巖巖納豪凱普阿米，為王女考埃萊米莫收養成婚。他借妻之手使父王自漁具葫蘆中取出竊鉤，再借十尋雙舟出海——鰆魚紛紛自躍入艙，滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: Fish-god Kuula cycle; place-name etymologies Kaumakapili and Nahakaipuami retained.

passages.text: Kuula was the father and Hina was the mother of Aiai; they lived in Niolopa, Nuuanu. Kuula and his wife were great fisher folks, and they had in their possession a pearl fish-hook of great value called Kahuoi. This pearl fish-hook was in the keeping of a bird called Kamanuwai, and it was kept at Kaumakapili; this pearl fish-hook was so enticing that every time Kuula went out for aku, outside of Mamala, upon seeing the hook they would jump into the canoes of their own accord - this fish was the food which this bird lived on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: While Kuula was out for aku one day outside of Mamala, Kipapalaulu the king of Honolulu also went out fishing; and when he came near the place where Kuula was fishing he saw the aku jumping into the canoes of Kuula of their own accord. Upon seeing this he made up his mind to steal this fish-hook Kahuoi, which in due time was carried out; this act not only deprived Kuula of his favorite hook, but the bird also hungered from loss of its food - through this seizure of the pearl hook by Kipapalaulu the bird went without any food; it would fly on its roosting place and go to sleep. It was because the bird Kamanuwai closed its eyes from hunger that the place where it lived was called Kaumakapili, and the place is so called to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time after this Hina conceived and in due time gave birth to a male child who was called Aiai; at the birth of the child the parents threw it into the stream just below Kaumakapili. The water carried the child to a rock called Nahakaipuami just below the Haaliliamanu bridge, where it is seen to this day, where it floated. Kipapalaulu was at this time living at Kapuukolo, where his palace was situated, with his daughter Kauaelemimo by name; one day at noon she went in bathing with her maids and discovered Aiai by a large rock. Kauaelemimo took the child as her own and brought it up. When Aiai grew into manhood he was very handsome, so Kauaelemimo took him to be her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a while she conceived a child and began to have a longing for some fish; so Aiai went out rod fishing along the coast, and after catching a few took the fish home and gave them to his wife. After the lapse of some twenty or thirty days Kauaelemimo had a longing for aku, so she told Aiai to go out aku fishing. Aiai upon hearing his wife's request asked her to go to her father Kipapalaulu and ask him for a pearl fish-hook; the wife consented and went to her father, who gave her one. When Aiai saw the fish-hook he said, 'This pearl fish-hook is worthless; the fish will not bite it; it will weary one's body for nothing.' The wife then asked him where she could get another, and Aiai replied: 'You go to your father and tell him there is a pearl fish-hook that will enrich the fishermen; it is in the fishermen's calabash of fishing utensils.' By this the husband wished to get possession of the pearl fish-hook Kahuoi which had been stolen from his father by Kipapalaulu. Upon coming to her father she asked for another pearl fish-hook; Kipapalaulu refused, saying, 'There is none left to give; that was the last pearl fish-hook I had which I gave you.' Kauaelemimo said, 'Aiai told me you had another one; it is in the fishermen's calabash of fishing utensils.' 'Yes, certainly there is one; I now remember it for the first time.' The calabash was then brought to the king, and when he looked in it he found the hook which he gave to his daughter; the wife then returned with it to her husband. Aiai took it and said, 'My days of poverty are now over since you have come back.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Aiai then said to his wife: 'Go back again to your father and ask him for a canoe; not one of five or eight fathoms in length, but get one that is ten fathoms in length; that is the size of the canoe that I want from your father.' When Kauaelemimo arrived in the presence of her father she asked for the canoe described by her husband; when the canoe ten fathoms in length was brought the father asked the daughter, 'Who will be able to paddle this canoe?' 'My husband will.' When Aiai heard the answer made by his wife he took the canoe and set out with the bird Kamanuwai, taking the pearl fish-hook Kahuoi along. When he arrived off of Mamala he took out the hook and began fishing; the aku began to come and jump into the canoe of their own accord until it was loaded down deep. The bird then ate some of the fish and was again restored to its former self. When Aiai came home his double canoe was loaded down deep with aku; upon arriving in the presence of his wife he gave her all the fish, but the pearl fish-hook was taken by the bird Kamanuwai, its guardian. This is the legend of Aiai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Pupualenalena, the Dog Who Stole Awa and the Spirits' Shell
title.zh: 竊卡瓦與奪神螺的義犬普普阿萊納萊納

region.zh: 夏威夷島普阿科至懷皮奧

texts.period: Hawaiian oral tradition (reign of Hakau); recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Pupualenalena, a dog of Puako, eats every fish his fisherman-master catches; the man bargains - eat away, if you bring me awa. Night after night the dog raids Hakau's awa field below the Puaahuku cliff in Waipio until the field is nearly gone and the king sets guards. Condemned with his master, the dog hears the king's price of pardon: the great shell Kuana, blown every night by the spirits above Waipio. At midnight it leaps the sleeping guards, hooks its head through the shell's loop and flees - one side striking a rock and breaking off, waking the spirits in vain chase. Master and dog become Hakau's favourites on a grant of land.
summary.zh: 普阿科的義犬普普阿萊納萊納食盡主人每尾漁獲；主人許諾——任你吃魚，只要為我取卡瓦。夜夜奔襲懷皮奧普瓦阿胡庫崖下的哈考王卡瓦田，直到田幾被掏空、國王設防。犬與主同判死刑；犬聽得王的赦免之價——懷皮奧上方群靈夜夜吹響的神螺庫阿納。午夜它躍過沉睡的守衛，頭穿螺繩而逃——螺觸巖缺角一聲，群靈驚起窮追不及。主犬終為哈考座上賓，得封地而居。

sensitivity.note: Animal-helper legend tied to Hakau (Umi's half-brother) cycle.

passages.text: Pupualenalena was a dog that once lived in Puako, Hawaii, with its own master. After a while his master was kidnapped by Kanikaa, a spirit, so the dog went and lived with another master; it was the usual thing for the new master to go out fishing, so he took the dog with him, making it sit behind him in the canoe. Every time a fish was caught the dog would eat it up, and as the dog kept on doing this for some time the master said: 'Yes, I have no objections to your eating the fish, if you can only supply me with my favorite drink, the awa, then it would be all right for you to eat the fish.' While the master was saying this the dog Pupualenalena understood him; in the evening the dog disappeared - this absence was because it went to steal awa down in the valley of Waipio. At this time Hakau the king was living at Waipio; he owned a large field of awa just at the foot of the Puaahuku cliff. This was the field where Pupualenalena came and got awa; at daybreak he would reach home with his awa, when his master would take it, cut it up and prepare some and drink it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The master after this had all the awa he wanted and the dog kept him supplied for many days; the dog, however, went to the place so often that after a while very little of the field was left, so Hakau began to be suspicious and therefore set guards over the field. While the guards were watching one night the dog came to the field and began pulling up the awa; when he had a sufficient amount for a load he took up the load and returned home. The guards then were sure that a dog was pulling the king's awa, so they followed it; the dog being much faster than the guards it got away, but one fellow who was a good runner kept up the chase until Pupualenalena was finally tracked to Puako. When the guard saw the dog's master he was covered with scales from the constant use of awa; the guard then approached him and asked, 'Say, is this your dog?' The master replied, 'Yes.' The guard then said, 'You two have sinned against the king, Hakau; your dog has been stealing the awa which belongs to the king.' The guard then took the man and his dog and brought them to Hakau in the valley of Waipio; when they arrived in the presence of Hakau he asked, 'Is this your dog?' 'Yes, it is mine', answered the man. Hakau asked, 'Have you been drinking my awa then?' 'Yes, I have been drinking it. I thought that the awa came from some place nearer home; but I am mistaken, and he has been getting it from Waipio here.' Hakau replied, 'Yes, I am going to kill both of you for taking my awa.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: During this time, in the reign of Hakau, there was a large shell used as a trumpet, called Kuana, that was owned by the spirits which lived above Waipio; this shell was blown every night and the sound from it made Hakau angry. So he said to the master of Pupualenalena: 'I will, however, save you and your dog if you will get me the shell owned by the spirits.' While Hakau was speaking Pupualenalena heard and understood the king's wish; that night the shell was again blown by the spirits. At midnight the king of the spirits retired, leaving the guards to keep watch; but later on they also fell asleep. Pupualenalena then stole in and jumped over the sleeping guards; seeing the shell hanging over the king it jumped over him, took the shell, stuck his head in through the loop of the string by which it was hung up and ran off with it. While in its flight and just as he was out of the house one side of the shell struck a rock and a piece of the shell was broken off; upon hearing the crack of the shell the spirits woke up and gave chase, but they were unable to catch the dog. When the dog arrived in the presence of Hakau with the shell he was so happy that he thereupon placed the master and his dog on a piece of land near by, and they became great favorites with Hakau.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.zh: 邁萊勞利伊與製鹽新郎

region.en: Kiholo to Kalahuipuaa, Kona, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島科納基霍洛至卡拉胡普瓦阿

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kaulanapokii (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: The five maile sisters of King Kaumalumalu sightsee down the Kona coast to Kalahuipuaa, where the perfectly formed Puako takes Mailelaulii to wife. At dawn the sisters see him hauling sea-water into salt-making pools and shrink from such lowly toil: 'If that is going to be your husband we will all be made weary' - and the marriage of the royal daughter to the salt-maker anchors the story of the salt ponds of Kalahuipuaa.
summary.zh: 國王考馬盧馬盧的五位邁蕾姊妹沿科納海岸遊歷至卡拉胡普瓦阿，遇上體貌完美的普阿科，長姊邁萊勞利伊與之成婚。翌日清晨姊妹們卻見他挑運海水灌注製鹽石池，頓生鄙意：『若要嫁這樣的丈夫，我們都得累死』——王室之女與製鹽人的這段姻緣，也就把卡拉胡普瓦阿鹽池的故事留在了島上。

passages.text: Kaumalumalu was the father and Lanihau the mother who once lived in Holualoa, Kona, Hawaii, residing there as king and queen at that time: Mumu was their first-born, then came Wawa, then Ahewahewa, then Lulukaina and then Kalino, making five sons; then came Mailelaulii, Mailekaluhea, Mailepakaha, Mailehaiwale, and last came Kaulanapokii, making five daughters. After the children were grown up Mailelaulii asked her younger sisters, saying: 'Let us go sight-seeing hereabouts.' They then started out and went as far as Huehue, from which point Kohala can be seen; on beholding the white sands of Kiholo and Kapalaoa they were enticed to go on; when they arrived at Kapalaoa they thought they would keep on to Kalahuipuaa; upon arriving at Kalahuipuaa they met Puako.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kaulanapokii (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puako was a very handsome man whose form was perfect; when he saw Mailelaulii he took her to be his wife, and that night they were covered with the same kapa. Very early the next morning the girls looked and saw Puako carrying sea water and filling pools for salt making; upon seeing this the sisters got disgusted and said to Mailelaulii: 'Say, if that is going to be your husband we will all be made weary' - the marriage of the royal daughter to the salt-maker anchoring the story of the salt ponds of Kalahuipuaa on the Kona coast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kaulanapokii (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.zh: 被擲下懸崖的勞基亞馬努伊卡希基

region.en: Coast cliffs of Hawaii Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島海岸懸崖（象徵性定位）

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Hina, daughter of the man- and wife-eating Laamaomao, bears Laukiamanuikahiki in secret; the child is directed to the cliff and cast from it with a bamboo float, surviving as the 'bird-of-many-fares' of the legend's name. She is found and reared by her grandparents, who send her back to her father's house - the opening movement of a cycle in which Hina admits to her the fate of her father's victims.
summary.zh: 食人男女的勞毛毛之女希娜祕密產下勞基亞馬努伊卡希基；嬰兒被引至崖邊，縛著竹浮筒擲入海中——卻如其名『多程之鳥』般倖存。祖父母尋得並撫養她，後送返父家；循此開端，希娜終向她吐露父親食人的真相，展開整個傳說的循環。

sensitivity.note: Cannibal-parent theme recorded as in source.

passages.text: Hina admits to Laukiamanuikahiki of her father: she was the daughter of Laamaomao, who ate both men and wives, and rearers of Laukiamanuikahiki were her grandparents - Hina and Makiioeoe, whose daughter Laukiamanuikahiki was. Her grandmother directs her to the cliff, and the bamboo as her float: the child, given birth to in secret, was cast from the cliff with the bamboo, and like the bird-of-many-fares whose name she carries survived the fall, to be found and brought up by the grandparents and returned to her father's house - where Hina tells her the fate of the victims of her father's table.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The name Laukiamanuikahiki means the leaf of the bird that flies from island to island - 'many-fares' - and the legend makes her the child who escapes the cannibal father's practice by being cast into the sea and saved: Hina, her mother, suffered the same appetite in her own household, and the story runs that the grandmother Hina, who had been thrown from the same cliff in her own infancy and survived, taught her granddaughter the bamboo-float trick that saved the second generation of the family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.
